tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

- Optional parameter `language` can filter results.

- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.

3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

# IPC hot spots: zarrow worktree zig-0-17-migration-branch-f92e21

Paths are relative to `C:\Users\cable\Documents\dev\zarrow\.claude\worktrees\zig-0-17-migration-branch-f92e21\`. All line numbers are ones I read.

## Copy summary
- **Read (stream, uncompressed):** body bytes are copied **once**, by `readSliceAll` into one 64-aligned body allocation (`src/ipc/stream_reader.zig:305-307`). Each buffer is then a zero-copy `body.slice(start,end)` (`:1238`), as long as `canReuseBodySlice` passes (`:1475-1480`). One extra cost: the body is zero-filled before that read (finding 1).
- **Write (stream):** body bytes are copied **once**, straight from each column's `SharedBuffer` into the sink with no intermediate buffer (`src/ipc/stream_writer.zig:339-343`). Metadata is copied twice: builder → `dupe` → sink (finding 3).
- **Schema:** decoded once in `readSchema` (`stream_reader.zig:183`) and shared per batch with `schema_ref.retain()` (`:220`). There are no per-batch DataType deep copies: `readArrayFromMeta` stores `dt` by value, pointing into the schema arena (`:1338`).
- **No O(n²) on the per-batch path.** Dictionary lookup is a hash map (`:1333`). The only quadratic spot is the vtable dedup search in `Builder.writeVtable` (`src/fbs_runtime/Builder.zig:167-186`). It is linear in vtables already written, so roughly O(F²) for a schema message with F fields, and that message is written once.

## Ranked findings

### 1. Whole body (and metadata) zero-filled, then overwritten — read path
- **Where:** `src/buffer.zig:152-160`, `OwnedBuffer.init`
  - `const data = try allocator.alignedAlloc(u8, ALIGNMENT_VALUE, actualCapacity);`
  - `@memset(data, 0);`
- **Called by:**
  - `readMessageOptional`, metadata (`stream_reader.zig:286-288`) and body (`:305-307`, `try self.reader.readSliceAll(body_buf.data[0..body_len]);`)
  - FileReader `readSharedAt` (`src/ipc/file_reader.zig:304-306`)
- **Why slow:** it adds a full write pass over every body byte, which is about 2x memory traffic for large batches.
- **Fix:** add `OwnedBuffer.initUninit(alloc, cap)` that only zeroes the tail padding, and use it at those call sites.
  - Before: `OwnedBuffer.init(a, n); readSliceAll(data[0..n])`
  - After: `initUninit(a, n)` with `@memset(data[n..], 0)`, then `readSliceAll(data[0..n])`
- **Risk:** low. Keep the tail zeroed, because `OwnedBuffer.typedSlice` exposes the full capacity (`buffer.zig:203-205`).

### 2. validateLayout runs twice per top-level column on read, and the columns array is allocated twice
- **Where:**
  - `stream_reader.zig:1345`, `readArrayFromMeta`: `try data.validateLayout();` (runs on every node)
  - `buildRecordBatchFromFlatbuf` (`:1145`, `:1180-1186`) calls `RecordBatch.init`, which validates again (`src/record_batch.zig:45-51`: `try data.validateLayout();`, `data_type.eql`, `hasNulls`)
  - It then allocates and retains a second columns array (`record_batch.zig:53-57`), and the caller releases and frees the first (`stream_reader.zig:1184-1186`).
- **Why slow:**
  - validateLayout is O(rows) for string/binary/list offsets (`validateOffsetsI32`, `src/array/array_data.zig:218-231`) and views (`validateByteViews`, `:272+`), so string-heavy batches scan their offsets twice.
  - Per batch it also costs one extra alloc/free plus 2 atomic ops per column.
- **Fix:** add an internal `RecordBatch.initOwnedValidated(alloc, schema_ref, columns)` that takes ownership of `columns`. It keeps only the length / type / nullable checks and skips validateLayout (the reader already validated at `:1345`).
- **Risk:** low. Keep the `:1345` check, since that is the trust boundary.

### 3. A new flatbuffer Builder per message, grown from 32 bytes, then dup'd
- **Where:** `src/ipc/fbs_lite/builder.zig:19-28`, `packMessageBytes`
  - `var builder = fb.Builder.init(allocator); defer builder.deinitAll();`
  - `return try allocator.dupe(u8, bytes);`
- **Called by:** `writeMessage`, `stream_writer.zig:329-335`
- **Why slow:**
  - `growByteBuffer` (`Builder.zig:261-281`) starts at 32 bytes and doubles, doing `std.mem.copyForwards` on every growth.
  - The `vtable` and `vtables` lists also allocate (`Builder.zig:123`, `:225`).
  - Then come the dupe, the write, and the free.
  - Net: about 5-8 allocs plus several memmoves per batch, for a few hundred bytes of metadata.
- **Fix:**
  - Keep `builder: fb.Builder` in StreamWriter, call `reset()` per message (`Builder.zig:101-110` already supports alloc-free reuse), and write `finishedBytes()` straight to the sink (no dupe).
  - Minimum version: `Builder.initCapacity(allocator, 1024)` (`Builder.zig:62`) and skip the dupe by writing inside `packMessageBytes`.
- **Risk:** low. `deinitAll` moves to `StreamWriter.deinit`.

### 4. Writer per-batch ArrayLists start at capacity 0 and grow one append at a time
- **Where:** `stream_writer.zig:261-264`
  - `var nodes = try std.ArrayList(fbs.FieldNodeT).initCapacity(self.allocator, 0);` (same for `buffers`, `variadic_buffer_counts`, `body_buffers`)
  - Appends in `appendArrayMeta` (`:1155`, `:1172`, `:1176`)
  - Same pattern in `writeDictionaryBatch` (`:908-911`)
- **Why slow:** growth is geometric, so not O(n²), but it costs about log2(n) reallocs × 4 lists per batch. The lists are then moved into `RecordBatchT` and freed by `msg.deinit` (`:302-316`).
- **Fix:**
  - Use `initCapacity(alloc, batch.columns.len)` for nodes and `2*cols+1` for buffers / body_buffers. This is exact for flat schemas.
  - Better: keep the lists in StreamWriter and reclaim them before `msg.deinit` (set `record_batch_ptr.nodes = .empty` etc. after `writeMessage`), then `clearRetainingCapacity`.
- **Risk:** none for the capacity hint; low for reuse.

### 5. Read path per-batch allocation inventory (flat schema, F primitive columns: about 9 + 2F allocs)
- Metadata: `OwnedBuffer.init` + `toShared` → `allocator.create(BufferStorage)` (`stream_reader.zig:286-289`, `buffer.zig:186`). That is 2 allocs.
- `unpackMessage`:
  - `create(RecordBatchT)` (`src/ipc_schema/org/apache/arrow/flatbuf/MessageHeader.fb.zig:129`)
  - nodes / buffers `initCapacity` (`RecordBatch.fb.zig:124`, `:135`)
  - That is 3 allocs.
- Body: 2 allocs (`:305`, `:308`).
- Columns: `alloc` (`:1145`), plus the `RecordBatch.init` copy (finding 2).
- Per column: `buffers` alloc (`:1213`) + `ArrayNode` create (`src/array/array_ref.zig:152`).
- **Fix (metadata):** use a reusable `meta_scratch: std.ArrayList(u8)` in StreamReader. The metadata `SharedBuffer` is released in `MessageWithBody.deinit` (`:276`) and never retained; the only `retain` calls are at `:220`, `:259`, `:1264`, `:1334`. That saves 2 allocs per batch.
- **Fix (body):** fold `BufferStorage` into the same allocation (header before the data) to save 1 alloc per buffer storage.
- **Risk:** low.

### 6. Compressed read: decompressed bytes copied up to 4x
- **zstd** (`stream_reader.zig:1636-1649`): `std.Io.Writer.Allocating` growth (`:1636-1641`), then `toOwnedSlice` (`:1643`), then `OwnedBuffer.init` (memset) + `@memcpy` (`:1647-1648`).
- **Then** `decodeRecordBatchBody` concatenates all parts into a new body:
  - `OwnedBuffer.init(allocator, cursor)` (memset #1)
  - `@memset(out, 0);` (memset #2, redundant)
  - `@memcpy(out[start .. start + len], decoded_parts[i].data[0..len]);` (`:1604-1611`)
- **LZ4** already allocates once at the exact size (`:1664`), answering your question 6 for that codec, but still goes through the concat copy.
- **Fix:** first pass sums `paddedLen(expected_len)` from each 8-byte header and allocates one uninitialized body. Second pass decompresses directly into `out[start..start+len]`: zstd through `std.Io.Writer.fixed(slot)` with `streamRemaining`, LZ4 by passing the slot pointer. Delete `decoded_parts` and the second memset.
- **Write side** (`stream_writer.zig:1237-1243`, `:1286`, `:1298`): compress into a bound-sized buffer, `realloc`, then `OwnedBuffer.init` + memcpy. Instead, compress directly into `OwnedBuffer(8 + bound).data[8..]`.
- **Risk:** medium, because of the offset bookkeeping.

### 7. FileWriter unpacks every message again and copies every body a second time
- **Where:** `src/ipc/file_writer.zig:79`: the StreamWriter writes into a `pending` Allocating buffer.
- Then `flushPendingMessages` does:
  - `var msg_t = try fbs_lite_builder.unpackMessage(self.allocator, metadata);` (`:203`) just to switch on `msg_t.header` (`:212`)
  - `try self.writer.writeAll(rest[0..message_total]);` (`:257`)
- **Why slow:** full flatbuffer unpack per message (allocs), and the body is copied twice (pending → sink).
- **Fix:** switch on `envelope.header_type` (already parsed at `:200`, map with `messageHeaderFromTypeTag`, `file_reader.zig:566`). Unpack only for Schema. Removing the second copy needs the StreamWriter to report block offsets (larger change).
- **Risk:** low for the header switch.

### 8. FileReader copies metadata and body out of an in-memory file on every batch
- **Where:** `file_reader.zig:287-307`, `readDecodedBlock` / `readSharedAt`
  - `const metadata = try self.allocator.alloc(u8, metadata_len);` + `@memcpy` (`:289-291`, `:312`)
  - Body: `OwnedBuffer.init` (memset) + memcpy (`:304-306`)
- **Fix:** pass metadata as a slice `self.bytes[start..end]`. `buildRecordBatchFromMessageMetadata` only takes `[]const u8` (`stream_reader.zig:680`). Body: use `initUninit` (finding 1).
- **Caveat:** a borrowed body via `SharedBuffer.fromSlice` would be *worse*, because `canReuseBodySlice` returns false when `storage == null` (`stream_reader.zig:1476`), so every buffer would be copied individually.
- **Risk:** low.

### 9. Builder debug logging: compiled out in Release, very expensive in Debug
- **Where:** `Builder.zig:90-97`, `fn debug(...)` → `std.log.debug(fmt, args);`. It is `std.log.debug`, not `std.debug.print`.
- **Called from:**
  - `place()` on every scalar written (`:612`)
  - `prep()` twice (`:307`, `:315`)
  - `prependUOff` (`:330`)
  - `createString` (`:404`)
- **Std gating (Zig 0.17 `lib/std/log.zig`):**
  - `:54-57` `.debug => .debug, .safe, .fast, .small => .info`
  - `:70` `if (comptime !logEnabled(level, scope)) return;`
- **Result:** comptime-eliminated in ReleaseFast, ReleaseSafe and ReleaseSmall. In Debug, every flatbuffer scalar write emits a stderr line. Nothing in `src/` or `build.zig` overrides `std_options` (grep found none), so **benchmark only in Release**.
- **Also:** `pad()` writes one byte at a time, `for (0..n) |_| b.place(u8, 0);` (`:289-291`). This is at most 7 bytes per `prep`, so minor; `@memset` on `bytes.items[head-n..head]` would replace it.
- **Fix:** delete the `debug()` body, or gate it on a comptime flag.
- **Risk:** none.

### 10. Per-batch schema walks on the writer, and user-side schema clones
- **Writer:** `writeRecordBatch` re-walks the schema for dictionary IDs on every batch (`stream_writer.zig:217-222`, `collectDictionaryIdsFromField`). Hoist it into `writeSchema` and cache the IDs; it is tiny for flat, dictionary-free schemas.
- **User side:** `RecordBatch.initBorrowed` (`record_batch.zig:68-71`) calls `SchemaRef.fromBorrowed`, which deep-clones the schema into an arena and builds a `field_index` hash map (`src/schema.zig:93-104`, `:231-238`). If the benchmark builds N batches this way, that is N schema clones.
- **Fix (user side):** create the `SchemaRef` once and call `RecordBatch.init(alloc, ref.retain(), cols)`.
- **Also:** `appendArrayMeta` popcounts validity when `null_count == null` (`stream_writer.zig:1154`). Builders that set `null_count` avoid this.

### 11. 128/256-bit types copied on read when their offset isn't 16/32-aligned
- **Where:** `primitiveValueAlignment` returns `@alignOf(i128)` / `@alignOf(i256)` for `interval_month_day_nano`, `decimal128` and `decimal256` (`stream_reader.zig:1399`, `:1402-1403`).
- IPC only pads buffers to 8 (`format.zig:11` `Alignment: usize = 8`, writer `paddedLen` at `stream_writer.zig:1177`).
- So on targets where `@alignOf(i128) > 8`, `canReuseBodySlice` (`:1478-1479`) can fail and fall back to `OwnedBuffer.init` + `@memcpy` (`:1240-1243`).
- **Fix (writer):** pad body offsets to 64 like Arrow C++. Or accept 8-aligned slices and read those types with unaligned loads.
- **Risk:** medium (writer format change; still spec-valid).

### Small reads/writes check (your item 3)
These are all fine:
- Length prefix: two 4-byte `readSliceAll` calls (`format.zig:28-37`, `:51-55`).
- Padding: `discardAll` on read (`:43-45`) and `splatByteAll` on write (`:39-41`).
- Body padding is written from an 8-byte stack array (`stream_writer.zig:338-342`).
- The only per-byte loop is `Builder.pad` (finding 9).

## Public API (`src/root.zig:58-70`)
Exports: `zarrow.IpcStreamWriter`, `zarrow.IpcStreamWriterOptions`, `zarrow.IpcStreamReader`, `zarrow.IpcStreamReaderOptions`, `zarrow.IpcFileWriter`, `zarrow.IpcFileReader`, `zarrow.IpcBodyCompressionCodec`. `zarrow.SchemaRef` is at `:48`, `zarrow.RecordBatch` at `:54`, `zarrow.Int32Builder` at `:139`.

**Writer** (`src/ipc/stream_writer.zig`):
```zig
pub fn init(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, writer: *std.Io.Writer) Self                              // :141
pub fn initWithOptions(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, writer: *std.Io.Writer, options: WriterOptions) Self // :149
//   WriterOptions{ body_compression: ?BodyCompressionCodec = null, endianness_mode = .strict, metadata_version = .v5 } // :125
pub fn writeSchema(self: *Self, schema: Schema) (WriterError || std.Io.Writer.Error)!void           // :186
pub fn writeRecordBatch(self: *Self, batch: RecordBatch) (WriterError || std.Io.Writer.Error)!void  // :216
pub fn writeEnd(self: *Self) std.Io.Writer.Error!void   // :321, writes EOS + flush()
pub fn deinit(self: *Self) void                          // :172
```

**Reader** (`src/ipc/stream_reader.zig`):
```zig
pub fn init(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, reader: *std.Io.Reader) Self                               // :137
pub fn initWithOptions(allocator, reader, options: ReaderOptions) Self                               // :146
pub fn readSchema(self: *Self) (...)!Schema    // :175; returned Schema lives in the reader's SchemaRef arena (valid until deinit / next readSchema)
pub fn nextRecordBatch(self: *Self) (...)!?RecordBatch // :194; null at EOS; caller owns -> batch.deinit()
pub fn deinit(self: *Self) void                 // :155
```

**Batch construction** (`src/record_batch.zig`): `init(allocator, schema_ref: SchemaRef, columns: []const ArrayRef) !Self` (`:40`; retains columns, takes ownership of `schema_ref`) and `initBorrowed(allocator, schema: Schema, columns) !Self` (`:68`; clones the schema). Free with `batch.deinit()` (`:75`).

**Shape to copy:**
- Test `"stream reader reads schema and batch through an unbuffered reader"`, `src/ipc/stream_reader.zig:323-365`. It uses `std.Io.Writer.Allocating`, `StreamWriter.init(allocator, &out.writer)`, then `writeSchema` / `writeRecordBatch` / `writeEnd`, then `std.Io.Reader.fixed(out.written())`, `readSchema`, `nextRecordBatch`, `deinit`.
- Full read loop with the public names: `examples/ipc_stream.zig:37-73`, for example `while (try reader.nextRecordBatch()) |*rb| { var out_batch = rb.*; defer out_batch.deinit(); ... }`.
- Tip: pre-size the sink with `std.Io.Writer.Allocating.initCapacity(allocator, n)` (std `Io/Writer.zig:2664`).
- There is no IPC benchmark in `benchmarks/` yet; it has only builder and csv benchmarks.

  - `var msg_t = try fbs_lite_builder.unpackMessage(self.allocator, metadata);` (`:203`) just to switch on `msg_t.header` (`:212`)
  - `try self.writer.writeAll(rest[0..message_total]);` (`:257`)
- **Why slow:** full flatbuffer unpack per message (allocs), and the body is copied twice (pending → sink).
- **Fix:** switch on `envelope.header_type` (already parsed at `:200`, map with `messageHeaderFromTypeTag`, `file_reader.zig:566`). Unpack only for Schema. Removing the second copy needs the StreamWriter to report block offsets (larger change).
- **Risk:** low for the header switch.

### 8. FileReader copies metadata and body out of an in-memory file on every batch
- **Where:** `file_reader.zig:287-307`, `readDecodedBlock` / `readSharedAt`
  - `const metadata = try self.allocator.alloc(u8, metadata_len);` + `@memcpy` (`:289-291`, `:312`)
  - Body: `OwnedBuffer.init` (memset) + memcpy (`:304-306`)
- **Fix:** pass metadata as a slice `self.bytes[start..end]`. `buildRecordBatchFromMessageMetadata` only takes `[]const u8` (`stream_reader.zig:680`). Body: use `initUninit` (finding 1).
- **Caveat:** a borrowed body via `SharedBuffer.fromSlice` would be *worse*, because `canReuseBodySlice` returns false when `storage == null` (`stream_reader.zig:1476`), so every buffer would be copied individually.
- **Risk:** low.

### 9. Builder debug logging: compiled out in Release, very expensive in Debug
- **Where:** `Builder.zig:90-97`, `fn debug(...)` → `std.log.debug(fmt, args);`. It is `std.log.debug`, not `std.debug.print`.
- **Called from:**
  - `place()` on every scalar written (`:612`)
  - `prep()` twice (`:307`, `:315`)
  - `prependUOff` (`:330`)
  - `createString` (`:404`)
- **Std gating (Zig 0.17 `lib/std/log.zig`):**
  - `:54-57` `.debug => .debug, .safe, .fast, .small => .info`
  - `:70` `if (comptime !logEnabled(level, scope)) return;`
- **Result:** comptime-eliminated in ReleaseFast, ReleaseSafe and ReleaseSmall. In Debug, every flatbuffer scalar write emits a stderr line. Nothing in `src/` or `build.zig` overrides `std_options` (grep found none), so **benchmark only in Release**.
- **Also:** `pad()` writes one byte at a time, `for (0..n) |_| b.place(u8, 0);` (`:289-291`). This is at most 7 bytes per `prep`, so minor; `@memset` on `bytes.items[head-n..head]` would replace it.
- **Fix:** delete the `debug()` body, or gate it on a comptime flag.
- **Risk:** none.

### 10. Per-batch schema walks on the writer, and user-side schema clones
- **Writer:** `writeRecordBatch` re-walks the schema for dictionary IDs on every batch (`stream_writer.zig:217-222`, `collectDictionaryIdsFromField`). Hoist it into `writeSchema` and cache the IDs; it is tiny for flat, dictionary-free schemas.
- **User side:** `RecordBatch.initBorrowed` (`record_batch.zig:68-71`) calls `SchemaRef.fromBorrowed`, which deep-clones the schema into an arena and builds a `field_index` hash map (`src/schema.zig:93-104`, `:231-238`). If the benchmark builds N batches this way, that is N schema clones.
- **Fix (user side):** create the `SchemaRef` once and call `RecordBatch.init(alloc, ref.retain(), cols)`.
- **Also:** `appendArrayMeta` popcounts validity when `null_count == null` (`stream_writer.zig:1154`). Builders that set `null_count` avoid this.

### 11. 128/256-bit types copied on read when their offset isn't 16/32-aligned
- **Where:** `primitiveValueAlignment` returns `@alignOf(i128)` / `@alignOf(i256)` for `interval_month_day_nano`, `decimal128` and `decimal256` (`stream_reader.zig:1399`, `:1402-1403`).
- IPC only pads buffers to 8 (`format.zig:11` `Alignment: usize = 8`, writer `paddedLen` at `stream_writer.zig:1177`).
- So on targets where `@alignOf(i128) > 8`, `canReuseBodySlice` (`:1478-1479`) can fail and fall back to `OwnedBuffer.init` + `@memcpy` (`:1240-1243`).
- **Fix (writer):** pad body offsets to 64 like Arrow C++. Or accept 8-aligned slices and read those types with unaligned loads.
- **Risk:** medium (writer format change; still spec-valid).

### Small reads/writes check (your item 3)
These are all fine:
- Length prefix: two 4-byte `readSliceAll` calls (`format.zig:28-37`, `:51-55`).
- Padding: `discardAll` on read (`:43-45`) and `splatByteAll` on write (`:39-41`).
- Body padding is written from an 8-byte stack array (`stream_writer.zig:338-342`).
- The only per-byte loop is `Builder.pad` (finding 9).
